outcome: A June 2025 preprint by Khyodeno Mozhui and K. V. Krishna proves the conjecture (attributed to Akgün et al.) that the crown graph H_{n,n} has the highest representation number among bipartite graphs on 2n vertices, for the case n odd (and for unequal-sized partite sets more generally); the case where both partite sets are equal and even remains open.
summary: The Wikipedia bullet asks whether crown graphs require the longest word-representants of all bipartite graphs — i.e., whether H_{n,n} has the maximum representation number among bipartite graphs on 2n vertices. This is precisely the conjecture attributed in the literature to Akgün et al. (building on the known fact, from Kitaev/Chen-type results on crown graphs, that H_{n,n} has representation number ⌈n/2⌉, the maximum possible for a comparability graph on 2n vertices). In arXiv:2506.01057 ("On the Conjecture of the Representation Number of Bipartite Graphs", submitted 1 June 2025), Khyodeno Mozhui and K. V. Krishna prove that every bipartite graph is (1+⌈m/2⌉)-representable (m = size of the smaller partite set) and, when m is odd, that it is ⌈m/2⌉-representable — matching or falling below the crown graph's bound in all cases except when both partite sets are equal and even in size. The paper's own introduction and conclusion state this explicitly: the crown-graph-maximality conjecture is established 'when n is odd', leaving the equal-even-size case open. I could not find any journal acceptance, expert digestion (e.g. a survey or Tao-style write-up), or a later paper closing the remaining even case; the live Word-representable graph Wikipedia article (fetched today) still lists the bullet as an open problem with no mention of this 2025 progress, and a search of Mozhui/Krishna's subsequent 2025-2026 publications (an upper-bound paper in J. Information Processing 2025, and 'Word-Representation of Melon Graphs' in Graphs and Combinatorics 2026) did not turn up a resolution of the even case. No AI system is credited anywhere in the paper, its abstract, or surrounding coverage; the methods described (neighborhood inclusion graphs, direct combinatorial construction) are entirely classical human mathematics. This is therefore a `partial` resolution: a genuine case-restriction (all bipartite graphs except one symmetric family) of the exact stated conjecture, settled in the conjectured (confirming) direction, with `ai_role` `none`.
competing_reading: One could argue this should be `open` with `no_change_found` if one reads the Wikipedia bullet as asking only about the single extremal question (which specific graph is the unique maximizer) rather than about the general upper bound — under a very strict reading, the 'crown graphs are extremal' claim is only proven for a subfamily (n odd, or unequal partite sets), not universally, so the conjecture itself is still technically open in full generality. I judge `partial` is the better fit because the paper explicitly frames its result as (partially) proving that specific named conjecture, and a strict majority of cases (all except equal-even) are now settled in the confirming direction — this is a textbook case of 'a case of the problem settled' under §3.1, not a variant problem.
what_would_settle_it: A paper (or the same authors' follow-up work) resolving the remaining case of bipartite graphs with equal, even-sized partite sets — either proving H_{n,n} (n even) still has the maximum representation number, or exhibiting a bipartite graph on 2n vertices (n even) with a strictly larger representation number than the crown graph, which would refute the conjecture and directly answer the Wikipedia bullet in the negative.
